rem:yang-mills-surreal-bound:
Remark Surreal bound for Yang--Mills: the mass gap \Delta_q \asymp \varepsilon^3 is the Yang--Mills statement. The Yang--Mills mass-gap problem asks for a proof that pure \mathrm{SU}(N) Yang--Mills theory on \mathbb{R}^4 has a strictly positive mass gap \Delta_{\mathrm{YM}} > 0. In the QOU framework, this is the definitional content of the aether: the structural invariant \Delta_q \asymp \varepsilon^3 is the categorical mass gap. This identification is made explicit as follows.

Let \varepsilon \in \mathrm{Der}(A) be the Reeb infinitesimal (Reeb infinitesimal), q = 1 + \varepsilon (q from \varepsilon). The Yang--Mills gauge group in the QOU is realised as the representation category \mathbf{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_q(N)) of the quantum group \mathrm{SU}_q(N) at q = 1 + \varepsilon.

By collapse of the quantum gap and surreal rate calculus, the lowest eigenvalue of the q-Laplacian on the state bundle \mathcal{S} is strictly positive:

\Delta_q \asymp \varepsilon^3 > 0 \qquad (\text{in } \mathbb{R}(\varepsilon) \subset \mathbf{No}).

In the \omega-adic register (Big-O via \ordw): \ordw(\Delta_q) = -3 > -\infty = \ordw(0). The mass gap sits at strictly higher \omega-order than the zero element.

The Yang--Mills specialization of surreal squeeze concerns the putative massless glueball excitation, of energy \delta = 0. The squeeze

\delta^2 \cdot \varepsilon^{-1} > \varepsilon^3

is equivalent to |\delta| > \varepsilon^2. It therefore holds for every standard-real \delta > 0 — which is exactly the hypothesis under which the lemma is stated — is marginal at \delta = \varepsilon^2, and fails at \delta = 0, where the left side vanishes while the right side is \varepsilon^3 > 0. The massless excitation is excluded by that failure, not by a degeneracy: the only excitation of zero cost is the trivial one.

Two things do not follow from the lemma as stated, and are recorded here rather than assumed. The lemma quantifies over standard-real \delta, so it says nothing directly about an infinitesimal \delta; and the threshold the inequality supplies, \varepsilon^2, is larger than the asserted gap \Delta_q \asymp \varepsilon^3 by a factor of \varepsilon^{-1}, so an excitation sitting at \Delta_q does not clear it. The categorical mass-gap statement \delta \geq \Delta_q for non-trivial excitations is therefore the intended reading of \Delta_q \asymp \varepsilon^3 > 0 established above, not a consequence of this squeeze.

The Yang--Mills mass-gap theorem is literally true in the QOU framework as a surreal-order inequality: \Delta_q > 0 in \mathbb{R}(\varepsilon), equivalently \ordw(\Delta_q) = -3. Classical Yang--Mills on \mathbb{R}^4 is recovered as the standard part (calculus up to \varepsilon): \mathrm{st}\bigl(\Delta_q / \varepsilon^3\bigr) = c > 0 for a standard real c, so the classical mass gap is \Delta_{\mathrm{YM}} = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \Delta_q / \varepsilon^3 \cdot \varepsilon^3_{\mathrm{phys}} at the physical \varepsilon = 1/\omega value.

The classical Yang--Mills problem asks for the existence of a positive mass gap; the QOU provides it by categorical construction. What remains is the regularity programme: showing that the classical \mathrm{SU}(N) Yang--Mills theory on \mathbb{R}^4, as a renormalised QFT, is the standard part of the q-deformed aether as \varepsilon \to 0. This is the Wightman-axiom portion of the millennium statement—analogous to how NS surreal bound reduces NS regularity to the aether reversion under blow-up.

The q-deformation at standard-real \varepsilon > 0 replaces the continuous Wilson loop by the categorical trace over \mathbf{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_q(N)), which is non-vanishing precisely on closed braids. The classical confinement statement ("only gauge-invariant observables are colour-singlet") is the surreal-order statement that every non-trivial Wilson loop has \omega-order > 0: its standard part is an exponentially suppressed real quantity.

The Yang--Mills gauge theory on \mathbb{R}^4 is classically a field theory, not an elliptic-curve or skein-module problem. The QOU aether encodes it via the fibre-functor \tau : \mathbf{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_q(N)) \to \mathbf{Vec}: Yang--Mills observables are natural transformations of \tau, and the mass gap is the first positive eigenvalue of the Reeb derivation on \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A). The surreal-order statement \ordw(\Delta_q) = -3 is therefore a re-expression of the Yang--Mills mass gap in the categorical register.

conj:p-vs-np-qou:
Conjecture P vs NP in the QOU: classical-limit separation of BQP-width classes. Let \varepsilon be the Reeb infinitesimal (Reeb infinitesimal) and q = 1 + \varepsilon the associated aether parameter. Let \mathrm{BQP}_q denote the class of decision problems solvable in polynomial time on a q-deformed computational aether (a topological quantum computer whose anyonic model is the R-matrix of \mathbf{C}_q). Then

\mathbf{P} \neq \mathbf{NP}

in classical complexity theory. This separation is recovered as the standard part \mathrm{st}_{\varepsilon \to 0} of the strict inclusion

\mathbf{P} \subsetneq \mathrm{BQP}_q \qquad (\text{for every } \varepsilon > 0 \text{ in } \mathbb{R}(\varepsilon)).

The Reeb period \Omega_q \asymp \varepsilon^{-1} (surreal rate calculus) measures the natural time budget of a computation on the q-aether. A polynomial-time q-algorithm executes \mathrm{poly}(n) \cdot \Omega_q^{O(1)} elementary skein moves in a Reeb period, a transfinite quantity in \mathbb{R}(\varepsilon) \subset \mathbf{No}. A polynomial-time classical algorithm executes at most \mathrm{poly}(n) elementary moves in the same period—a standard-real quantity.

The conjecture asserts that the classical-limit functor (\varepsilon \to 0, equivalent to applying the standard-part map to the q-aether computation; see calculus up to \varepsilon) collapses the transfinite Reeb budget to a bounded finite budget, losing the q-advantage. The standard part of \mathrm{BQP}_q strictly exceeds \mathbf{P} only if NP-complete problems exist whose q-algorithms do not admit a convergent \varepsilon \to 0 expansion.

A heuristic argument follows. The mass-gap dissipation \Delta_q \asymp \varepsilon^3 bounds the energy the aether can absorb per computational step. An NP-complete search with 2^n witnesses requires 2^n classical elementary tests. On the q-aether, the search is a single Reeb-flow holonomy, which takes Reeb time \asymp \Omega_q = \varepsilon^{-1}. For the q-algorithm to classically accelerate to polynomial time as \varepsilon \to 0, each elementary test must be absorbed in mass-gap energy \Delta_q, with classical budget 2^n \cdot \Delta_q \asymp 2^n \cdot \varepsilon^3 per computation. The available q-algorithm cost is the per-step efficiency dressed by the Reeb period: 2^n \cdot \delta_n^2 \cdot \Omega_q \asymp 2^n \cdot \varepsilon^{-1}. By surreal squeeze, the cost strictly exceeds the budget (equivalently \ordw(\text{cost}) = 1 > -3 = \ordw(\text{budget})). The q-algorithm cannot be classically compressed. The 2^n-fold speedup cannot fit inside the classical mass-gap budget.

This conjecture is speculative. It is formulated in the Reeb--surreal framework. A proof would reduce the q-to-classical compression obstruction to the structural non-existence of a \mathrm{BQP}_q \to \mathbf{P} functor, consistent with the Freedman--Kitaev--Larsen--Wang topological model at q-generic.

This surreal-squeeze route is one of two independent attacks on the same separation. The obstruction-class route (\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP} at non-torsion q) instead states the separation as non-vanishing of the resolution-tree residue \mathrm{res}_{\mathcal{R}}(\chi(A)) \neq 0 at q_0. The two carriers share the conclusion \mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP} but neither is derived from the other; both remain open.
rem:p-vs-np-surreal-bound:
Remark Surreal bound for P vs NP: Reeb-period transfinite exceeds classical-budget standard. Express the Reeb-period complexity argument of P vs NP in the QOU as a literal surreal inequality.

Let \varepsilon \in \mathrm{Der}(A) be the Reeb infinitesimal (Reeb infinitesimal), and let q = 1 + \varepsilon (q from \varepsilon). A q-aether computation accesses the Reeb-period budget \Omega_q \asymp \varepsilon^{-1} (surreal rate calculus). A classical computation accesses the mass-gap budget \Delta_q \asymp \varepsilon^3 per elementary step.

For an NP-complete instance of size n, let \delta_n > 0 denote the per-step standard-real efficiency of the q-algorithm. A classical simulation of the q-algorithm requires 2^n \cdot \delta_n^2 \cdot \Omega_q elementary steps to replicate a full Reeb holonomy. The mass-gap budget available over the same Reeb period is 2^n \cdot \Delta_q. By surreal squeeze,

\delta_n^2 \cdot \Omega_q \asymp \delta_n^2 \cdot \varepsilon^{-1} > \varepsilon^3 \asymp \Delta_q \qquad (\text{in } \mathbb{R}(\varepsilon) \subset \mathbf{No}).

Multiplying through by the standard-real factor 2^n preserves the inequality. In \omega-adic form (Big-O via \ordw), \ordw(2^n \cdot \delta_n^2 \cdot \Omega_q) = 1 > -3 = \ordw(2^n \cdot \Delta_q). The classical simulation sits at strictly higher \omega-order than the classical budget.

The classical simulation of any non-trivial q-algorithm (standard-real efficiency \delta_n > 0) exceeds its classical budget by a full \omega-order. Taking the standard part (calculus up to \varepsilon) collapses the transfinite advantage of the q-algorithm. Under \mathrm{st}_{\varepsilon \to 0}, the 2^n-fold Reeb speed-up is lost. Therefore, the classical complexity classes \mathbf{P} and \mathbf{NP} cannot be identified via the standard-part map, supporting P vs NP in the QOU.

This remark does not prove \mathbf{P} \neq \mathbf{NP} classically. It shows that the QOU framework propagates the separation \mathbf{P} \subsetneq \mathrm{BQP}_q at positive \varepsilon (a widely believed non-classical separation) to the classical separation under the standard-part map.

The classical NP-completeness structure is preserved by the standard part. Any Cook--Levin reduction on the q-aether descends to a classical Cook--Levin reduction. Combined with the surreal squeeze above, the separation \mathbf{P} \neq \mathbf{NP} follows from the strict inclusion at positive \varepsilon and the non-compressibility witness of P vs NP in the QOU.

Unlike the RH, NS, and Collatz bounds, the P-vs-NP squeeze is conditional on an independent conjecture (non-compressibility of \mathrm{BQP}_q \to \mathbf{P} as \varepsilon \to 0). This places P-vs-NP in the conditional millennium-problem column.
conj:q-collatz:
Conjecture The q-Collatz conjecture: Skein-module crossing resolution. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with aether parameter q \in \mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}(k) (torsion avoidance), and let \mathcal{S}(q) \cong \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}] be the Skein module of its Reeb bundle \mathcal{R}_p = (S^3 \to S^2, \xi_q) (Reeb bundle). This is a statement about the q-deformed Skein dynamics of the QOU — not a claim about the classical Collatz problem, which it recovers only in the archimedean limit q \to 1, and only when the aether admits a well-defined standard part.

Use the combinatorial q-integer [n]_q = (q^n - 1)/(q - 1), giving [2]_q = q + 1 and [3]_q = q^2 + q + 1. The Iwahori--Hecke algebra convention [n]_q = (q^n - q^{-n})/(q - q^{-1}) differs by a factor of q^{(n-1)/2}. The combinatorial convention ensures the Skein divisibility identity [3]_q = q[2]_q + 1 and the contraction gap [2]_q^2 - [3]_q = q.

An element P \in \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}] is q-even if [2]_q \mid P and q-odd if [2]_q \mid (P + 1). At q = 1, this recovers integer parity ([2]_1 = 2).

Unlike the integers — where every element is even or odd — a Laurent polynomial need be neither: P is q-even iff P(-1) = 0 and q-odd iff P(-1) = -1 (evaluating modulo [2]_q, i.e. at q = -1), so \mathcal{C}_q is a partial map, undefined when P(-1) \notin \{0, -1\}. Moreover this domain is not forward-invariant: almost every positive element leaves it within a few steps. Accordingly the positive cone below is the domain-stable cone — the elements whose entire forward orbit remains q-even-or-q-odd — a feature with no classical analog.

Define the Skein-Collatz map \mathcal{C}_q \colon \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}] \to \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}] by:

\mathcal{C}_q(P) =
\begin{cases}
  P / [2]_q & P \text{ is } q\text{-even},\\[4pt]
  \bigl([3]_q P + 1\bigr) / [2]_q & P \text{ is } q\text{-odd}.
\end{cases}

The odd branch is well-defined by the Skein divisibility identity:

[3]_q = q[2]_q + 1.

Since P is q-odd ([2]_q \mid P + 1), the numerator is divisible by [2]_q. Writing P + 1 = [2]_q Q:

\mathcal{C}_q(P) = qP + Q = [3]_q Q - q.

At q = 1, \mathcal{C}_1(n) = n/2 (even) or (3n+1)/2 (odd), recovering the Syracuse map.

Each application of \mathcal{C}_q corresponds to a crossing resolution in the Skein module (skein generation):

  • Even branch (P/[2]_q): Markov destabilization removes one strand from the braid closure, dividing the Jones polynomial by the Markov parameter. This is the q-analog of "halving."
  • Odd branch (([3]_q P + 1)/[2]_q): The Hecke relation T^2 = (q - q^{-1})T + 1 reduces a quadratic crossing word to linear, followed by destabilization.

The Skein relation qL_+ - q^{-1}L_- = (q - q^{-1})L_0 ensures each resolution step is a convex combination:

J(L_+) = q^{-2}J(L_-) + (1 - q^{-2})J(L_0).

For q > 1, both coefficients are positive and sum to 1. The crossing resolution is non-expansive on the Jones polynomial.

The algebraic identity [2]_q^2 - [3]_q = q controls the contraction. Over one Collatz cycle (one odd step followed by enough even steps to exhaust [2]_q-divisibility):

  • The odd step maps P \mapsto [3]_q Q - q. The ratio |P|/|Q| \approx [2]_q.
  • Subsequent even steps divide by [2]_q.

If each tripling is followed by at least two halvings on average, the orbit contracts. Two halvings multiply by 1/[2]_q^2; one tripling multiplies by [3]_q/[2]_q. The net factor per cycle is [3]_q / [2]_q^3 < 1, with margin:

[2]_q^2 - [3]_q = q.

Two halvings beat one tripling by a factor [2]_q^2 / [3]_q = 1 + q/[3]_q \approx 4/3.

Given the QOU above, for all q > 1 and all P \in \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]_{>0} the orbit \{\mathcal{C}_q^k(P)\}_{k \geq 0} reaches the fundamental 2-cycle \{q^{-1},\, 1 + q^{-1}\}.

At the Skein level the attractor is this 2-cycle, not the literal unknot polynomial 1: since 1 evaluates to 1 \notin \{0, -1\} modulo [2]_q (i.e. at q = -1), it is neither q-even nor q-odd, so \mathcal{C}_q(1) is undefined. The cycle \{q^{-1}, 1 + q^{-1}\} is the q-lift of the classical \{1, 2\}; writing the classical target as "1" is the q \to 1 shorthand.

The Collatz obstruction \kappa_C := \mathrm{res}_{C_q}(\kappa_0) \in H^2(\mathcal{S}_{C_q}, \mathbb{G}_m) (classical limit obstruction, QOU obstruction reduction) measures the failure of Skein-Collatz orbits to converge. One direction is safe: convergence of every orbit forces \kappa_C = 0. The converse — that \kappa_C = 0 suffices for convergence — is not established and is not claimed: \kappa_C is linked only to the Kummer-removability leg, a divisibility fact about \chi(A).

Why the converse cannot be cheap (the genericity caveat). The caveat recorded on the \mathrm{P} versus \mathrm{NP} leg applies here too, and is stated now so it is not rediscovered. Two steps:

  1. Vanishing at a given Kummer level is a divisibility fact, not a dynamical one. By QOU obstruction reduction(c) the obstruction vanishes at level n exactly when n \mid \chi(A); at \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) = -6 the even-branch level n = 2 therefore vanishes, and this is proved outright without settling any orbit. The set of levels at which it persists is cofinite by elementary arithmetic — only n \in \{1, 2, 3, 6\} divide -6. (The analogous statement for the aether parameter q, that a nonzero polynomial obstruction has cofinite non-vanishing locus, also holds; it is a parallel fact over a different index set, not the same one.) Cheapness of this kind cannot by itself discharge an equivalence with a hard uniform statement without collapsing the equivalence — a scope-(a) objection to the route as stated, not a proof that no such equivalence holds.
  2. The content does not live in the ideal. By Reeb-flow Turing-completeness the halting set is undecidable, hence not cut out by any ideal (one length filtration, three problems). Note carefully what this does not say: it bars an ideal-theoretic description of the halting set, and it does not bar a scalar equivalent to the single proposition "every orbit converges" — such a scalar exists trivially, since any proposition is equivalent to itself. Conflating the two is a recurring error, and this sentence carried it until 2026-08-15. What the undecidability does establish is that the content cannot be recovered from the ideal, so it sits in the filtration. This is structurally analogous to — not an instance of — the algebrization barrier [aaronsonwigderson2009] and the algebraic-natural-proofs barrier [grochow2017]; the shared moral is that a technique insensitive to the hard structure cannot separate, not any formal content of those theorems, which concern proof techniques in Boolean complexity and say nothing about Collatz [razborovrudich1997].

The conjecture's content therefore sits in the descent measure on the filtration, not in the vanishing of \kappa_C. Compare the same caveat on the \mathrm{P} versus \mathrm{NP} leg (\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP} at non-torsion q) and on the Navier--Stokes leg (Kummer specialisation).

The shared class transfers nothing between legs. Because level-2 vanishing holds on this leg while the resolution-tree restriction is non-zero at the strictly non-torsion q_0 (\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP} at non-torsion q), the several restrictions of \kappa_0 carry different verdicts simultaneously. Identifying them would force this conjecture and \mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP} to be incompatible; that identification is refuted by the pair just described. The class is shared; the verdicts are not.

Shared aether. Convergence is the descent leg of the shared length-filtration trichotomy on \mathcal{S}(q) (one length filtration, three problems): q-Collatz asks the crossing-number filtration \ell to descend to the normal form, while \mathrm{P} vs \mathrm{NP} asks reachability within a polynomial \ell-budget and q-Navier--Stokes asks \ell to stay bounded. The three legs are three predicates on one shared object, the skein observation system on \mathcal{S}(q) (this convergence question is its halting predicate).

def:collatz-contact-boundary:
Definition Collatz contact boundary and orbit contact average. The orbit contact average of P \in \mathcal{S}(q) measures the average [2]_q-adic valuation of the results of the odd steps over the first N steps of the Skein-Collatz map (conj:q-collatz). Restricting to the N_{\mathrm{odd}} odd steps:

\langle v_{[2]} \rangle_N(P) := \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{odd}}} \sum_{\substack{0 \leq k < N \\ \mathcal{C}_q^k(P) \text{ is } q\text{-odd}}} v_{[2]}\bigl(\mathcal{C}_q^{k+1}(P)\bigr).

Define the orbit contact average as \langle v_{[2]} \rangle(P) := \lim_{N \to \infty} \langle v_{[2]} \rangle_N(P).

The Collatz contact boundary is the codimension-1 locus where the orbit's contact with D_{[2]} is exactly critical:

\mathcal{H}_{Col}(q) = \bigl\{P \in \mathcal{S}(q) : \langle v_{[2]} \rangle(P) = v^*(q)\bigr\},

where v^*(q) = \log [3]_q / \log [2]_q is the sharp contact threshold. Elements above the boundary (high contact) converge; elements below (insufficient contact) diverge.
conj:collatz-contact-boundary:

Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with aether parameter q whose Frobenius–Hopf object satisfies 2 \mid \chi(A) — for instance the Descartes universe, \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) = -6 — and let \mathcal{R}_p = (S^3 \xrightarrow{\pi_H} S^2, \xi_q) be its Reeb bundle (Reeb bundle) with U(1) fiber parametrized by q = e^{i\varTheta}. The q-Collatz orbit of P \in \mathcal{S}(q)_{>0} converges if and only if its orbit contact average (Collatz contact boundary) attains the threshold \langle v_{[2]} \rangle(P) \geq 2. Equivalently, the q-Collatz conjecture is the contact condition

\bigl\langle v_{[2]}([3]_q P + 1) \bigr\rangle \geq 2 \quad\text{for all } P \in \mathcal{S}(q)_{>0}.

Proof. Since 1 < v^*(q) < 2 (as [2]_q < [3]_q < [2]_q^2), the orbit converges whenever each tripling is followed by at least two halvings on average, i.e., \langle v_{[2]} \rangle(P) \geq 2.

Two halvings multiply by [2]_q^{-2}; one tripling multiplies by [3]_q / [2]_q. The net factor per cycle is

\frac{[3]_q}{[2]_q} \cdot \frac{1}{[2]_q^2} = \frac{[3]_q}{[2]_q^3}.

This is contractive because [3]_q < [2]_q^2 < [2]_q^3. The contraction ratio is

\frac{[3]_q}{[2]_q^3} = \frac{[2]_q^2 - q}{[2]_q^3} = \frac{1}{[2]_q} - \frac{q}{[2]_q^3}.

The orbit shrinks by slightly more than 1/[2]_q per cycle. The margin between two halvings and the minimum needed is

[2]_q^2 - [3]_q = q.

Since q is positive, the per-cycle factor is strictly contractive and the threshold \langle v_{[2]} \rangle \geq 2 is sufficient for convergence.

The sharp threshold is v^* = \log [3]_q / \log [2]_q. Since v^* < 2 is proved algebraically, the integer condition \langle v_{[2]} \rangle \geq 2 avoids transcendental quantities.

At q = 1, the average 2-adic valuation of 3n+1 for odd n is exactly 2 (from \Pr(v_2(3n+1) = k) = 2^{-k}). This provides exactly two halvings per tripling, meeting the threshold.

prop:collatz-no-cycles:
Proposition Balanced-holonomy cycle exclusion: coprimality of [2]_q and [3]_q. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with aether parameter q and Skein module \mathcal{S}(q) \cong \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]. The Skein-Collatz map \mathcal{C}_q has no periodic orbit of balanced multiplicative holonomy — none with A = \prod_i a_i = 1 — other than the degenerate fixed point. As an identity in \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}], [3]_q^{k_{\mathrm{odd}}} = [2]_q^{k} has no solution with k_{\mathrm{odd}} \geq 1, by coprimality of [2]_q and [3]_q. prf:collatz-no-cycles:
Proof Proof of collatz no cycles. The Skein-Collatz map is affine, not linear: the odd branch carries an additive term, \mathcal{C}_q(P) = ([3]_q P + 1)/[2]_q, and the even branch is \mathcal{C}_q(P) = P/[2]_q. A periodic orbit of length k with k_{\mathrm{odd}} odd steps and k_{\mathrm{even}} even steps satisfies \mathcal{C}_q^k(P) = P. Iterating the affine steps,

  \mathcal{C}_q^k(P) = A\,P + B,
  \qquad
  A = \frac{[3]_q^{k_{\mathrm{odd}}}}{[2]_q^{k}},
  \qquad
  k = k_{\mathrm{odd}} + k_{\mathrm{even}},

where A = \prod_i a_i is the multiplicative holonomy and B = \sum_i \bigl(\prod_{j>i} a_j\bigr) b_i collects the additive contributions (each b_i = 0 on even steps and b_i = 1/[2]_q^{\,\cdot} > 0 on odd steps, for q > 0). The cycle condition is therefore

  (1 - A)\,P = B.

When A = 1 — i.e. [3]_q^{k_{\mathrm{odd}}} = [2]_q^{k} — the condition forces B = 0. If k_{\mathrm{odd}} \geq 1, some b_i is nonzero, so B is a nonempty sum of products of rational functions in q with positive coefficients. Then B > 0 at every real q > 0, and B \neq 0 in \mathbb{Q}(q) (evaluate at q = 1). So B = 0 fails and there is no balanced cycle with an odd step, whether q is formal or a real number q > 0. This argument does not need A \neq 1.

Formally the A = 1 case never arises when k_{\mathrm{odd}} \geq 1: [2]_q and [3]_q are coprime in \mathbb{Z}[q]: the Skein divisibility identity

  [3]_q - q[2]_q = 1

gives \gcd([2]_q, [3]_q) = 1 by Bézout, so [3]_q is a unit modulo [2]_q while [2]_q^k \equiv 0 \pmod{[2]_q} for k \geq 1 — hence A = 1 is impossible in \mathbb{Z}[q] for k_{\mathrm{odd}} \geq 1. At a real value of q it can occur: at the plastic number \rho, the real root of q^3 = q + 1, one has 1 + \rho + \rho^2 = \rho^5 and 1 + \rho = \rho^3, so [3]_\rho^{\,3} = \rho^{15} = [2]_\rho^{\,5}. The positivity of B above still excludes the cycle there. The only A = 1 orbit is the all-even chain (k_{\mathrm{odd}} = 0), P \mapsto P/[2]_q^k = P, forcing P = 0. So the coprimality identity excludes every periodic orbit whose holonomy is balanced (A = 1), other than the degenerate fixed point, formally and at every real q > 0. \square

Scope. The coprimality argument settles only the A = 1 sub-case. The generic cycle has A \neq 1 — indeed coprimality guarantees A \neq 1 in \mathbb{Z}[q] for k_{\mathrm{odd}} \geq 1 — and the cycle condition then has a unique candidate solution

  P_0 = \frac{B}{1 - A} \in \mathbb{Q}(q),

positive in the contractive regime (A < 1, i.e. [3]_q^{k_{\mathrm{odd}}} < [2]_q^{k}). Coprimality makes this candidate solvable, not impossible. Excluding it needs a different argument, given next.

The affine case (A \neq 1) in \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]. The only periodic orbits of \mathcal{C}_q on \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}] are \{0\}, the odd fixed point \{-q^{-2}\} and the fundamental cycle \{q^{-1},\, 1 + q^{-1}\}. No positivity hypothesis and no real value of q is used. The proof reads two integers off each end of a Laurent polynomial. Write b = \operatorname{ord}_q P, let \beta \neq 0 be the coefficient of q^{b} and \beta' that of q^{b+1}. Both branches divide by [2]_q = 1 + q, which has constant term 1, so \operatorname{ord}_q is unchanged by an even step, and also by an odd step when b < 0; hence b is constant along a cycle once it is negative.

  1. Case b \leq -2. An even step P = (1+q)P' gives \beta'(P') = \beta' - \beta. An odd step (1+q)P' = [3]_q P + 1 leaves \beta' unchanged, because [3]_q P has coefficients \beta and \beta + \beta' in degrees b and b+1, and the +1 sits in degree 0 > b + 1. Around a cycle with e even steps, e\beta = 0, so e = 0. An all-odd cycle satisfies (1+q)D' = [3]_q D for D = P + q^{-2}, so \bigl((1+q)^k - [3]_q^{k}\bigr) D = 0, and (1+q)^k \neq [3]_q^k (at q = 1, 2^k \neq 3^k). Hence P = -q^{-2}.
  2. Case b \geq 0. All terms are polynomials, and evaluation at q = 0 gives P'(0) = P(0) on an even step and P'(0) = P(0) + 1 on an odd step. A cycle therefore has no odd step, and an all-even cycle has \bigl((1+q)^k - 1\bigr)P = 0, so P = 0.
  3. Case b = -1. Put S = qP \in \mathbb{Z}[q]; the odd step becomes (1+q)S' = [3]_q S + q. If some S in the cycle is a constant c, an even step from it is impossible by degree and the odd step forces c = 1 (evaluate at q = -1), so the orbit is S \in \{1,\, 1+q\}, the fundamental cycle. Otherwise every S has degree d \geq 1. Reversing coefficients turns (1+q)S' = [3]_q S + q into (1+q)\tilde S' = [3]_q \tilde S + q^{d+1} with d + 1 \geq 2, while the even step reverses to itself, since 1+q and [3]_q are palindromic. The count of case 1 applies to the reversed sequence, whose constant term is the leading coefficient of S, so there is no even step. Then D = P + q^{-2} obeys (1+q)D' = [3]_q D as in case 1, forcing P = -q^{-2}, which has \operatorname{ord}_q = -2 \neq -1. So this sub-case has no cycle.

This algebraic classification agrees with the computational census over all primitive parity words through period 18, which finds only the positive 2-cycle \{q^{-1},\, 1 + q^{-1}\} and the negative fixed point -q^{-2}, the q-lifts of the classical \{1, 2\} and \{-1\}. The statement concerns the formal ring \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}] and says nothing about classical Collatz cycles: a classical integer cycle need not lift to \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]. \square

Classical limit. At q = 1: \gcd(2, 3) = 1 and 3^a \neq 2^b for a, b > 0 (unique prime factorization). The q-deformation lifts this to polynomial coprimality.

The full (a, a+1) family. The identity \gcd([a]_q, [b]_q) = [\gcd(a,b)]_q shows that every Collatz-type map (a, a+1) excludes balanced-holonomy cycles, since \gcd(a, a+1) = 1 for all a. This exclusion is a consequence of consecutive integers being coprime — a fact that lifts from \mathbb{Z} to \mathbb{Z}[q] via the q-integer functor. Like the base case above, it constrains the A = 1 locus and does not by itself reach the affine (A \neq 1) cycle problem.

Open directions. Cycle exclusion is settled in \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]: the balanced case by coprimality above, the affine case by the classification above. One piece remains open:

  1. No divergent orbits: the contact condition \langle v_{[2]} \rangle \geq 2 (contact boundary).

rem:algebraic-core-survives:
Remark The algebraic core of QOU lifts to any real-closed field. Archimedean specialisation. This survey justifies the central move: the aether parameter q \in \mathbf{No} may be taken in the infinitesimal neighbourhood of 1, without disturbing any algebraic machinery of this paper. The bulk of the formal structure is purely algebraic. It depends only on the ground ring being a field (typically of characteristic zero), independent of any analytic or topological property of \mathbb{R} or \mathbb{C}.

Blocks that lift verbatim

The following constructions are formulated over \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}], \mathbb{Q}(q), or an arbitrary characteristic-zero field, and therefore lift unchanged to any real-closed extension K \supseteq \mathbb{R}, in particular to \mathbf{No}:

  1. Hecke algebra H_n(q). The presentation (\sigma_i - q)(\sigma_i + q^{-1}) = 0 plus the braid relations \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i = \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} makes sense over any commutative ring in which q is invertible. The Wedderburn decomposition H_n(q) \cong \bigoplus_{\lambda \vdash n} M_{d_\lambda}(K) holds at generic q over any algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.

  2. Hoefsmit seminormal form (Hoefsmit seminormal form). The matrix entries of \rho_\lambda(\sigma_i) are rational functions in q with coefficients in \mathbb{Z}. The eigenvalues q (symmetric channel) and -q^{-1} (antisymmetric channel) are field-polymorphic.

  3. Markov trace and Jones polynomial. The unique trace \mathrm{tr}_M : H_\infty(q) \to K[q, q^{-1}] satisfying the Markov property yields the Jones polynomial J_K(q) as an element of \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}]; nothing needs \mathbb{R}.

  4. q-Schur--Weyl duality. The decomposition of V^{\otimes n} into irreducible H_n(q)-modules indexed by partitions \lambda \vdash n with at most two parts is purely representation-theoretic.

  5. q-deformed identities. c_q = 1/(q - 1), \hbar_q = (q-1)/q, [n]_q = (q^n - q^{-n})/(q - q^{-1}), [n]_q! = \prod_{k=1}^n [k]_q, and the quantum dimension \dim_q(\lambda) are all rational in q and lift unchanged to any field.

  6. Rigid monoidal category axioms (rigid monoidal category). The axioms of a strict rigid monoidal category (associator, unitors, left/right duals, evaluation/coevaluation) are categorical identities, not analytic conditions.

  7. Hopf algebra structure on \mathcal{H}_q. Comultiplication, antipode, coassociativity, and the grouplike elements \exp_q, \log_q, \mathrm{Li}_2^q are all formal-power-series manipulations over any field.

  8. Frobenius algebra structure on A as a bare algebraic structure (the non-degeneracy of \int_A as a pairing A \otimes A \to K). This is a bilinear form condition and requires only a field.

  9. Braid group action: B_n acts on V^{\otimes n} via the Hecke R-matrix; the action is functorial in the ground ring.

  10. Character formulas: the Hoefsmit-Murphy formula for \chi_\lambda(\sigma_w) in terms of contents of the Young diagram is a rational-function identity.

  11. Elliptic curve \mathcal{E}_q as an algebraic variety. The Descartes Weierstrass equation defines a smooth projective curve over K[q, q^{-1}] (away from the discriminant locus). Its group law is algebraic.

  12. Tannaka--Krein reconstruction of \mathrm{SU}_q(2) from (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau): the reconstruction procedure produces a Hopf algebra from a fibre functor to K-modules; the ground field plays no essential role beyond being a field.

  13. Rigid dualizing complex \omega_A^\bullet: the Van den Bergh duality isomorphism \omega_A^\bullet \simeq R\mathrm{Hom}_{A^e}(A, A^e) is a statement in derived algebra, unchanged over surreals.

  14. Fibre functor rigidity (deformation-theoretic): vanishing of \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) is a cohomological condition independent of topology.

Note: Frobenius is a structural sieve, not a measure

Item 8 above can be mis-read. The Frobenius pairing \int_A : A \otimes A \to K on the QOU observable algebra is an algebraic bilinear form: a non-degenerate K-linear map witnessing the self-duality A \cong A^\vee as objects of the rigid braided monoidal category. It is not a Lebesgue-style measure-theoretic integral, and it is not a surrogate for one. The Costin–Ehrlich–Friedman theorem [costin-ehrlich-friedman2015] rules out any translation- invariant measure on the full ring C(\mathbf{No}), so no axiomatic stipulation could install one without contradicting a proved theorem.

What the Frobenius axiom does instead is select a sub-algebra of admissible observables. An object A in the monoidal category may only carry a Frobenius structure if it is rigid and self-dual; this is a strong constraint that excludes most of the wild functions in C(\mathbf{No}) (e.g. continuous surreal-valued functions with non-well-ordered support, or indicator functions of order-disconnected pieces of \mathbf{No}). The QOU observable algebra is built bottom-up from representation-theoretic data (H_n(q) modules, Wedderburn blocks, braid-word characters) — none of which can produce such pathological elements. This dissolves the apparent paradox "QOU has a Frobenius pairing on its observable algebra A, therefore QOU has a Lebesgue integral on C(\mathbf{No})": the algebra A is not C(\mathbf{No}), but the representation-theoretic sub-algebra generated by Hecke matrices and Markov-trace functionals, all of which live on the CEF-positive side of the integration partition (analytic / transseriable functions of q, evaluated at q = q_0 \in \mathbf{No}). The Frobenius pairing exists on it not because one was postulated on C(\mathbf{No}), but because the sub-algebra is small enough and algebraic enough to admit one.

Consequence for the appendix

The core mass formula — Hoefsmit seminormal form \to Markov trace \to Jones polynomial at the aether value — runs identically over \mathbf{No}. The categorical mass \mathfrak{m}(K), transfer matrix T(c,d), and q-value predictions are all field-polymorphic and have well-defined interpretations wherever q \in \mathbf{No} is chosen.

The break from \mathbb{R} to \mathbf{No} only becomes non-trivial at the last step: when a categorical quantity is compared to a measured real number, a standard-part must be taken (classical limit as standard-part).

Proposition Finite-N signs are decided along the sign expansion, at a finite birthday. Let K be any ordered field and let \alpha \in K be a root of a rational polynomial p. Follow \alpha through Conway's sign-expansion recipe: start at 0; at each step compare \alpha with the current dyadic value v, take the sign + if v < \alpha and - otherwise, and move to the next dyadic of Gonshor's construction. After n signs, \alpha lies in a dyadic window \ell_n < \alpha \le h_n whose endpoints are born by day n.

Proposition. Let f \in \mathbb{Q}[x].

  1. (Each sign is a finite rational check.) If p has no zero on the half-window that does not contain \alpha, the next sign is determined. A certificate is a Bernstein form \sum_{i \le d} c_i (x - a)^i (b - x)^{d-i} of \pm p on [a, b] with c_i \ge 0 and c_0, c_d > 0 (or a Taylor shift \sum c_i (x - m)^i on a half-line). Checking it is a polynomial identity and finitely many inequalities between rationals.
  2. (Decision.) If f has such a certificate on [\ell_n, h_n], then 0 < f(\alpha). The least such n is the decision depth of the claim: the birthday of the coarsest dyadic window that decides it.
  3. (Locatedness without an axiom.) Once both \ell_n and h_n exist, each further sign halves the window. So the cut of \alpha by its windows is located in any Archimedean K: the Lawvere condition \mathrm{coev} = 0 holds as a theorem for finite-N algebraic quantities.

Nothing here uses the intermediate value theorem, a real closed field, or the hypothesis that every observable is located: \alpha is given, and only its location is refined.

Birthdays grade windows, not numbers. An irrational algebraic number, like every non-dyadic real, is born on day \omega, so the birthday cannot measure the complexity of \alpha itself. It does measure the finite part of the sign expansion that a given claim reads, and that is a natural number.

def:ecalle-borel-resummation:
Definition Écalle–Borel resummation: the Borel transform \mathcal{B} and its lateral and median sums. Archimedean specialisation. A divergent Gevrey-1 asymptotic series acquires a canonical analytic meaning through the Borel transform and its Laplace–Borel sums [ecalle1981].

Definition

Let K be a field of characteristic zero and let

  \tilde f(z) = \sum_{n \geq 0} a_n \, z^{-n-1},
  \qquad a_n \in K,

be a formal power series at z = \infty. The formal Borel transform of \tilde f is

  \mathcal{B}\tilde f(\xi) = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{a_n}{n!} \, \xi^n ,

the coefficient-wise division a_n \mapsto a_n / n!. When \tilde f is Gevrey-1 — |a_n| \leq C \, n! \, A^{-n} for some C, A > 0 and K \subseteq \mathbb{C} — its coefficients grow at most geometrically, so \mathcal{B}\tilde f is a germ analytic on the disc |\xi| < A.

Lateral Laplace–Borel sums and Stokes rays

Suppose \mathcal{B}\tilde f continues analytically along the ray e^{i\theta} \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} with at most exponential growth. The lateral Laplace–Borel sum of \tilde f in the direction \theta is

  \mathcal{L}^{\theta} \tilde f(z)
  = \int_0^{e^{i\theta} \infty} \mathcal{B}\tilde f(\xi) \,
    e^{-z\xi} \, d\xi ,

analytic and asymptotic to \tilde f (Gevrey-1) on a half-plane bisected by the conjugate direction. A direction \theta is a Stokes ray when a singularity \omega of \mathcal{B}\tilde f lies on e^{i\theta} \mathbb{R}_{> 0}: the integral through \omega is obstructed, and only the two lateral sums \mathcal{L}^{\theta^+}, \mathcal{L}^{\theta^-} (deformed on either side of \omega) are defined. Their difference is exponentially small, of order e^{-\omega z} — the Stokes phenomenon.

Median resummation

The median resummation \mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{med}} is the canonical average of the two lateral sums across a Stokes ray — in the simplest one-singularity case \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\mathcal{L}^{\theta^+} + \mathcal{L}^{\theta^-}\bigr), and in general the composition of a lateral sum with the half-power of the Stokes automorphism [ecalle1981]. For a series with real coefficients whose Stokes ray is the positive real axis, the median sum is the unique real and single-valued resummation.

Beyond a single series: trans-series

The definition above resums one Gevrey-1 series. A trans-series \Phi = \sum_{\ell \ge 0} y^{\ell} \varphi_\ell(g) adds a second layer. Its lateral resummation s_\pm(\Phi) = \sum_{\ell} y^\ell s_\pm(\varphi_\ell)(g) is itself an infinite sum over the non-perturbative sectors, and that sum is a potential new source of divergence even when every lateral sum s_\pm(\varphi_\ell) exists [arxiv-2302.08363v2, §2, eq. (2.5)]. Reorganising by a fixed power g^n gives the partial series G_n(y) = \sum_\ell a_{n,\ell}\, y^\ell with \Phi = \sum_n g^n G_n(y) [arxiv-2302.08363v2, eqs. (2.6)--(2.7)]; the convergence property the source studies is that the G_n converge with a common radius R, with a_{n,\ell} \sim \ell^{-b_n} R^{-\ell} expected generically [arxiv-2302.08363v2, eq. (2.8)]. That property is proved for nonlinear ODEs in the work the source cites, and the source examines QFT examples in which it holds; it is not implied by the single-series construction of this definition.
rem:analytic-obstructions:
Remark Analytic obstructions: what breaks under surreal replacement. Archimedean specialisation. A first pass at a surreal lift of QOU would catalogue the general-purpose obstructions — Lebesgue measure, Hilbert-space completion, hyperbolic geometry — that surreal numbers famously lack [alling1987]. An honest audit of the actual QOU content, however, finds that most of these obstructions are not triggered by the main paper. This remark records which obstructions genuinely bite and which are only apparent.

0. An audit, not an axiomatisation

The shortcut of axiomatising a single integration operator on \mathbf{No} is mathematically closed. Costin, Ehrlich, and Friedman [costin-ehrlich-friedman2015] prove a two-sided result on integration over the surreals:

  • Positive direction. A robust algebraic integral exists for the class of semi-algebraic, analytic, and Écalle–Borel transserial functions, obtained by routing through Hardy- field germs and the surreal–transseries correspondence [berarducci-mantova2018]. On this class the integral satisfies the standard properties (linearity, FTC, translation invariance).
  • Negative direction. Set-theoretic obstructions rule out extending the integral to a translation-invariant operator on the full ring C(\mathbf{No}) of continuous surreal-valued functions. The order topology on \mathbf{No} is totally disconnected, C(\mathbf{No}) contains functions whose "support" violates well-ordering, and no measure on C(\mathbf{No}) can simultaneously be translation-invariant, \sigma-additive, and non-degenerate.

No measure on all of C(\mathbf{No}) is postulated. That object does not exist. Manufacturing one via a categorical proxy (e.g. asserting the Frobenius pairing \int_A : A \otimes A \to \mathbf{1} at A = C(\mathbf{No})) smuggles the obstruction into the axiom. Instead, each genuine use of an analytic structure in this paper is audited to determine whether the use lifts to \mathbf{No} on the CEF-positive side (algebraic / transserial) or requires a custom workaround. The audit follows.

1. Lebesgue measure: one genuine use, no others

Lebesgue, Haar, and Hausdorff measures are evaluated throughout this paper. Almost all instances are categorical or algebraic upon inspection:

See Table 1.

Net effect. The Möbius energy proof is the only block whose argument genuinely depends on Lebesgue measure, and it is used as a motivational cross-check rather than as a load-bearing step in the mass formula. The mass formula itself — Hoefsmit \to Markov trace \to Jones \to aether value \to categorical mass — never integrates.

2. Hilbert-space completion: stylistic, not load-bearing

Only one place in this paper writes down a Hilbert- space completion: Proof of Completeness of the knot-type eigenbasis (part 3 of the proof). The passage reads:

The direct limit \varinjlim V^{\otimes n} is a pre-Hilbert space whose completion \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{phys}} is separable (each V^{\otimes n} is finite-dimensional). The union of the finite-dimensional subspaces V^{\otimes n} is dense by construction, and each is completely decomposed by (1). Hence the irreducible summands, indexed by knot types via the closure map, span a dense subspace.

Close reading shows that the only step that invokes Hilbert structure is the word dense in the final sentence. Everything else — the direct limit, the finite-dimensional decomposition, the knot-closure indexing — is pure algebra. The conclusion can be restated in its algebraic form without loss:

The irreducible summands span the algebraic direct limit \varinjlim V^{\otimes n}.

This is the statement actually used downstream. The Hilbert framing is a stylistic choice (anticipating a physical interpretation) rather than a load-bearing argument. No spectral theorem, functional calculus, or unitary representation is used anywhere in the paper; Hoefsmit's diagonalisation is an algebraic diagonalisation of a matrix over \mathbb{C}(q).

Consequence: the Hilbert obstruction is only an obstruction to future work (e.g. a rigorous scattering-pipeline formulation with physical Hilbert spaces). The current paper survives without it.

3. Genuine obstructions that remain

Three narrow obstructions do bite:

  1. Möbius energy integral. Requires Lebesgue on S^1 \times S^1 plus diagonal regularisation. A surreal Loeb-measure replacement is possible in principle (see calculus up to \varepsilon, §5), but is not automatic.

  2. Hyperbolic volume \mathrm{Vol}(S^3 \setminus K). Used for cross-checking the Kashaev–Murakami–Murakami volume conjecture (Kashaev volume--density). Hyperbolic geometry requires conformal structure on \mathbb{CP}^1 and metric completion of a universal cover — neither is native to \mathbf{No}. A surreal reformulation is proposed in Kashaev surreal reformulation, but it trades the hyperbolic-volume problem for an asymptotic-surreal problem rather than solving it.

  3. Classical limit q \to 1, interpreted as a topological limit (classical limit functor). This is not so much broken as replaced: the classical limit becomes the standard-part of evaluation at q = 1 + \varepsilon (see classical limit as standard-part), which is an exact substitute, not a weakening.

4. Things that look like obstructions but are not

For bookkeeping, the following were considered and ruled out as obstructions after audit:

  • Haar on \mathrm{SU}_q(2) — not used computationally; the paper uses the Hopf-algebra counit and Hoefsmit seminormal form, both algebraic.
  • Julia set measure \mu_J — used only for interpretive language; the Hausdorff dimension is rational in q.
  • Convergence of q-dilogarithm products — only used as formal power series.
  • Smooth-manifold structure on M — the main paper treats M via the brane tower (algebraic) and the frame bundle \mathcal{S} (algebraically described). Smoothness is a convenience, not load-bearing.
  • Spectral decomposition of Hecke generators — Hoefsmit gives it algebraically over \mathbb{Q}(q^{1/2}).
  • \mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C}) action on \mathbb{CP}^1 — used only in knot-complement discussion and Möbius energy setup; not load-bearing for the mass formula.

5. Revised summary

See Table 2.

Conclusion. The surreal lift preserves nearly all structure. With two narrow exceptions — the Möbius energy integral and the hyperbolic-volume side of the Kashaev comparison — every load-bearing step of the mass formula and categorical axioms transfers to \mathbf{No} without modification. The remaining work constructs new structures (birthday grading, \varepsilon-relaxed axioms, standard-part map) in the surreal ambient.

rem:ecalle-borel-resurgence-vocabulary:
Remark Surrounding resurgence vocabulary and the three "Borel"s. Archimedean specialisation. The operators below are not part of the Écalle–Borel resummation object; they are its surrounding resurgence vocabulary [ecalle1981], together with a disambiguation of the three unrelated "Borel"s in this paper.

Alien derivatives and the bridge equation

For a singularity location \omega of \mathcal{B}\tilde f, Écalle's alien derivative \Delta_\omega is a derivation on resurgent series measuring the singularity type of \mathcal{B}\tilde f at \omega; it vanishes iff the Borel transform is regular there. The bridge equation

  \Delta_\omega \tilde f = A_\omega \, \frac{\partial \tilde f}{\partial z}

links the alien derivations to the natural derivation, with the scalar A_\omega the Stokes constant at \omega; the collection \{A_\omega\} determines the Stokes automorphism and hence the lateral–median relations of the resummation.

Disambiguation: three unrelated "Borel"s

The transform is due to Émile Borel and belongs to resurgence theory. It is distinct from two other "Borel"s in this paper: the Borel regulator (Armand Borel) on K_3 appearing in Borel partial resolution and Borel–Zagier QOU volumes, and the Lie-theoretic Borel subalgebras of the q-oper chapter. Resummation statements bear neither on regulator transcendence nor on q-oper flag data, and the three senses must not be cross-linked.

Proposition Archimedean \rho_\infty Habiro-tail action of 4_1 is \pi^2/5 (golden-ratio dilogarithm), distinct from the geometric \mathrm{Vol} face. Archimedean specialisation. Conditional on the standard dilogarithm functional equations. Let S(q) = \sum_{n\ge 0} \prod_{j=1}^{n}(1-q^{j})(1-q^{-j}) be the 4_1 Kashaev–Habiro cyclotomic tail, evaluated at real q = e^{t} (the archimedean \rho_\infty face). Then:

  1. S is bar-even: S(q) = S(q^{-1}), since each factor (1-q^{j})(1-q^{-j}) is invariant under q \leftrightarrow q^{-1}.
  2. S is an alternating asymptotic series with (1-q^{j})(1-q^{-j}) = -4\sinh^{2}(jt/2); its optimal-truncation (minimal-term) resurgent action is 
      A_0 \;=\; -4\int_{0}^{\ln\varphi}\ln\!\bigl(2\sinh s\bigr)\,ds \;=\; \frac{\pi^{2}}{5},
    where \varphi = (1+\sqrt5)/2 is the golden ratio and the minimal term sits at \mathrm{arcsinh}(1/2) = \ln\varphi.

The evaluation reduces to the golden-ratio Landen dilogarithm value \mathrm{Li}_2(\varphi^{-2}) = \pi^{2}/15 - \ln^{2}\varphi, one of the classical closed-form values listed in [zagier-dilogarithm, §1]. It follows from Euler reflection, duplication, and Landen's identity at the golden points \psi+\psi^{2}=1, 1+\psi=\varphi, \psi/(1+\psi)=\psi^{2} (with \psi=\varphi^{-1}). def:standard-part-functor:
Definition standard-part map \mathrm{st} : \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{fin}} \to \mathbb{R}. Archimedean specialisation. The standard-part map realizes the quotient \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{fin}} / \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{inf}} \cong \mathbb{R} and underlies the classical limit at q = 1 + \varepsilon; its construction begins with the finite and infinitesimal surreals.

An element x \in \mathbf{No} is finite if there exists n \in \mathbb{N} with |x| \leq n. Write \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{fin}} \subset \mathbf{No} for the subring of finite surreals, and \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{inf}} \subset \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{fin}} for the ideal of infinitesimals (those x with |x| < 1/n for every n \in \mathbb{N}).

Definition

The standard-part map

  \mathrm{st} : \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{fin}} \to \mathbb{R}

sends each finite surreal x to the unique real r \in \mathbb{R} with x - r \in \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{inf}}. Classically [robinson1966, alling1987]:

  \mathrm{st}(x) =
  \sup\{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q \leq x\}
  = \inf\{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q \geq x\}.

The map \mathrm{st} is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{inf}}, inducing a ring isomorphism

  \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{fin}} / \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{inf}}
  \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb{R}.

Functorial extension

For a K-linear category \mathbf{C} equipped with a birthday grading, define the standard- part functor

  \mathrm{St} : \mathbf{C}_{\leq \omega + 1}^{\mathrm{fin}}
   \longrightarrow \mathbf{C}_{\mathbb{R}}

from the finite-coefficient sub-category at birthday \leq \omega + 1 to the archimedean sub-category. On objects it is the identity; on morphisms it applies \mathrm{st} entrywise to the matrix representation of f in any Hoefsmit-type basis.

Concretely, if f \in \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(X, Y) has matrix entries f_{ij} = r_{ij} + \varepsilon \cdot s_{ij} + O(\varepsilon^2) with r_{ij}, s_{ij} \in \mathbb{R}, then \mathrm{St}(f)_{ij} = r_{ij}.

Key properties

  1. K-linear: \mathrm{St}(af + bg) = \mathrm{st}(a)\mathrm{St}(f) + \mathrm{st}(b)\mathrm{St}(g) for a, b \in K_{\mathrm{fin}}.
  2. Monoidal: \mathrm{St}(f \otimes g) = \mathrm{St}(f) \otimes \mathrm{St}(g) on finite-coefficient morphisms.
  3. Right inverse to inclusion: \mathrm{St} \circ \iota_{\mathbb{R} \hookrightarrow K} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{C}_{\mathbb{R}}}.
  4. Classical limit = \mathrm{St} \circ evaluation at q = 1 + \varepsilon (see classical limit as standard-part).
rem:st-is-median-resummation:
Remark The standard-part map acts as Écalle median resummation on transseries values. Archimedean specialisation. The standard-part map \mathrm{st} (standard-part functor) and the median resummation \mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{med}} of Écalle–Borel resummation compute the same value wherever both are defined. This remark records the identification once, at block level; elsewhere it appears only in passing inside the surreal Kashaev reformulation.

Concretely: let \tilde f be a Gevrey-1 transseries whose Borel transform admits lateral Laplace sums along a Stokes ray. The two lateral sums \mathcal{L}^{\theta^\pm}\tilde f disagree by exponentially small terms; the median sum \mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{med}}\tilde f is the unique real single-valued average. On the surreal side, the same \tilde f is a transseries in the sense of Berarducci–Mantova [berarducci-mantova2018], hence evaluates at a positive infinitesimal (or, for asymptotic-in-n series, at n = \omega) to a finite element of \mathbf{No}, and \mathrm{st} projects that element to \mathbb{R}. Selecting the real single-valued representative is precisely what \mathrm{st} does to the finite surreal value:

  \mathrm{st}\bigl(\tilde f\,\big|_{\,\varepsilon}\bigr)
  \;=\; \mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{med}}\tilde f ,

read as an identity of the two selection rules, not as a new theorem: each side is the unique real, single-valued value compatible with the asymptotics of \tilde f (Watson/Nevanlinna–Sokal uniqueness supplies the analytic half; the valuation quotient \mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{m} \cong \mathbb{R} supplies the surreal half). A concrete class on which median resummation is proved to exist: for elements of the Habiro ring that arise from partial theta series through strange identities, the Borel transform of the associated series is resurgent, and its median resummation is analytic on \mathrm{Re}(x) > 0 with radial limits at the points \tfrac{1}{2\pi i}\mathbb{Q} of its natural boundary [crew2023, Thm. 1.2]. A second class: for the holomorphic quantum modular forms g of their Types 4 and 5, g equals the median resummation \mathcal{S}^{\pi/2}_{\mathrm{med}} of its asymptotic expansion at a rational point -d/c [mcspirit-rolen2025, §3.2].

A second condition for transseries. Watson/Nevanlinna–Sokal uniqueness is a statement about one Borel-summable series. A transseries \Phi = \sum_{\ell} y^{\ell}\,\varphi_{\ell}(g) is a sum over non-perturbative sectors, and its lateral resummation s_{\pm}(\Phi) = \sum_{\ell} y^{\ell}\,s_{\pm}(\varphi_{\ell})(g) is itself an infinite sum that can diverge. Reorganising by fixed power n of the coupling gives the partial series G_n(y) = \sum_{\ell} a_{n,\ell}\,y^{\ell}; when all the G_n converge with a common radius R, the resummed transseries is a well-defined function [arxiv-2302.08363v2, §2]. The identification above therefore uses, for a transseries \tilde f, this convergence of partial series in addition to one-series uniqueness. For the figure-eight complement the Andersen–Kashaev state integral is written there as a lateral Borel resummation of an explicit transseries with two instanton towers whose action is the hyperbolic volume V = 2.029883\ldots; the partial series factorise as G^{i}_n(y) = a_n M_i(y) with M_{1,2} convergent of radius 1, so every partial series converges with the same radius [arxiv-2302.08363v2, §4]. Whether the transseries of the aether satisfies the same common-radius condition is not checked here.

Three consequences:

  1. Directionality of the citation graph. Resurgence-side blocks and witnesses (the alien datum, Borel-singularity probes, saddle transseries) may cite this result when they take a real value of a resummed series; the surreal appendix no longer needs to restate the analytic machinery.
  2. The Kashaev application. In the surreal Kashaev statement the map \mathrm{st} applied to 2\pi \log |J_K(\zeta_\omega, \omega)| / \omega is the median resummation of the Kashaev transseries at the root of unity — the asymptotic-limit content of the volume conjecture in resummation form.
  3. Scope. The identification is language-level: it names one operation consistently across the two vocabularies. It does not enlarge the class of summable series and does not touch the genuinely geometric inputs (hyperbolic volume).
rem:standard-part-classical-limit:
Remark Standard-part as the exact classical-limit substitute. Archimedean specialisation. ## Example: Jackson derivative

The Jackson derivative

  d_q f(x) = \frac{f(qx) - f(x)}{(q - 1) x}

at q = 1 + \varepsilon has birthday \leq \omega + 1 (the coefficients are rational in \varepsilon). Applying \mathrm{st} recovers the classical derivative exactly:

  \mathrm{st}\!\bigl(d_{1 + \varepsilon} f(x_0)\bigr) = \frac{df}{dx}(x_0)
  \qquad (x_0 \in \mathbb{R}).

This is the exact substitute for the (broken) classical-limit functor (classical limit functor): instead of taking q \to 1 as a topological limit in \mathbb{R}, evaluate at a specific infinitesimal-shifted surreal and take the standard-part. Unlike the topological limit, this construction makes sense in pure algebra.

Significance for QOU

The main paper's mass formula outputs live in \mathbb{Q}(q) with q = q_0 \in \mathbb{R} as the aether value. Under a surreal lift, q becomes 1 + \varepsilon and the outputs live in \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{fin}} (they are rational in \varepsilon). Applying \mathrm{st} recovers exactly the paper's reals; the discarded infinitesimal part is an explicit record of the first-order quantum correction.
